# [2401.07883] The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator

[View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.07883) [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1)
> Abstract:Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) has become one of the most popular paradigms for enabling LLMs to access external data, and also as a mechanism for grounding to mitigate against hallucinations. When implementing RAG you can face several challenges like effective integration of retrieval models, efficient representation learning, data diversity, computational efficiency optimization, evaluation, and quality of text generation. Given all these challenges, every day a new technique to improve RAG appears, making it unfeasible to experiment with all combinations for your problem. In this context, this paper presents good practices to implement, optimize, and evaluate RAG for the Brazilian Portuguese language, focusing on the establishment of a simple pipeline for inference and experiments. We explored a diverse set of methods to answer questions about the first Harry Potter book. To generate the answers we used the OpenAI's gpt-4, gpt-4-1106-preview, gpt-3.5-turbo-1106, and Google's Gemini Pro. Focusing on the quality of the retriever, our approach achieved an improvement of MRR@10 by 35.4% compared to the baseline. When optimizing the input size in the application, we observed that it is possible to further enhance it by 2.4%. Finally, we present the complete architecture of the RAG with our recommendations. As result, we moved from a baseline of 57.88% to a maximum relative score of 98.61%.

# The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator

*Leonardo Avila Rodrigo Castaldoni Pedro Gengo Celio Larcher Marcos Piau Pablo Costa Vinicius Caridá

email: {pfinardi, leonardo.bernardi.avila, castaldoniro, pedro.gengo.lourenco, celiolarcher, marcos.piau.vieira, pablo.botton.costa, vfcarida}@gmail.com  
∗ Both authors contributed equally to this research.

###### Abstract

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) has become one of the most popular paradigms for enabling LLMs to access external data, and also as a mechanism for grounding to mitigate against hallucinations. When implementing RAG you can face several challenges like effective integration of retrieval models, efficient representation learning, data diversity, computational efficiency optimization, evaluation, and quality of text generation. Given all these challenges, every day a new technique to improve RAG appears, making it unfeasible to experiment with all combinations for your problem. In this context, this paper presents good practices to implement, optimize, and evaluate RAG for the Brazilian Portuguese language, focusing on the establishment of a simple pipeline for inference and experiments. We explored a diverse set of methods to answer questions about the first Harry Potter book. To generate the answers we used the OpenAI’s gpt-4, gpt-4-1106-preview, gpt-3.5-turbo-1106, and Google’s Gemini Pro. Focusing on the quality of the retriever, our approach achieved an improvement of MRR@10 by <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="35.4\%" intent=":literal" id="abstract1.m1"><semantics><mrow><mn>35.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">35.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 35.4%35.4\% compared to the baseline. When optimizing the input size in the application, we observed that it is possible to further enhance it by <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="2.4\%" intent=":literal" id="abstract1.m2"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 2.4%2.4\%. Finally, we present the complete architecture of the RAG with our recommendations. As result, we moved from a baseline of <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="57.88\%" id="abstract1.m3"><semantics><mrow><mn>57.88</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">57.88\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 57.88%57.88\% to a maximum relative score of <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="98.61\%" id="abstract1.m4"><semantics><mrow><mn>98.61</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">98.61\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 98.61%98.61\%.

## 1 Introduction

The rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) has changed the way we approach Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications. Their ability to answer different user queries in different domains allow these models to show a notable performance in a wide range of tasks like translation, summarizing, question answering, and many others [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib1 "")]. However, there are a lot of open challenges when it comes to problems that require answers based on updated information, and external data, that were not available in the training data.

In order to overcome this challenge, a technique called Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) [[2](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib2 "")] was developed. This approach aims to solve the limitation of the need for external data, by fetching and incorporating this information in the prompt. With this, the model can generate more cohesive answers about subjects and data not seen during the training, decreasing the occurrence of hallucinations [[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib3 "")]. Nevertheless, this approach adds a new layer of challenges since it requires the development of a trustworthy retriever pipeline, given that the quality of the final answer can be highly affected if the retrieved text is not relevant to the user query [[4](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib4 "")].

The landscape of RAG is rapidly expanding, with a constant influx of new papers introducing diverse implementations [[5](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib5 "")]. Each of these variants proposes technical modifications or enhancements, such as different retrieval mechanisms, augmentation techniques, or fine-tuning methodologies. This proliferation, while a testament to the field’s dynamism, presents a substantial challenge for AI practitioners. The task of methodically experimenting with, and critically evaluating, each variant’s performance, scalability, and applicability becomes increasingly complex.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive series of experiments focused on the application of RAG specifically tailored for Brazilian Portuguese. Our research delves into evaluating various retrieval techniques, including both sparse and dense retrievers. Additionally, we explore two chunking strategies (naive and sentence window) to optimize the integration of retrieved information into the generation process. We also investigate the impact of the positioning of documents within the prompt, analyzing how this influences the overall quality and relevance of the generated content. Finally, our experiments extend to comparing the performance of different LLMs, notably GPT-4 and Gemini, in their ability to effectively incorporate the retrieved information and produce coherent, contextually accurate responses. This paper aims to provide valuable insights and practical guidelines for implementing RAG in Brazilian Portuguese.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows: 1) we propose a methodology to prepare a dataset in a format that allows quantifying the quality of the different steps in an RAG system. 2) We proposed a metric (maximum relative score) that allow us to direct quantify the existent gap between each approach and a perfect RAG system. 3) We discuss and compare different implementations, showing good practices and optimizations that can be used when developing a RAG system.

## 2 Data Preparation

The chosen dataset was the first Harry Potter book in its Brazilian Portuguese version. This choice is motivated since it is a well known book, and both the Gemini Pro and OpenAI models can answer general questions on the subject. Additionally, over the application of the standard ChatGPT tokenizer cl100k_base, we observed that there are approximately <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="140,000" display="inline" id="S2.p1.m1"><semantics><mn>140,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">140,000</annotation></semantics></math> --> 140,000140,000 tokens in total, allowing the creation of prompts containing the entire book. Following, a dataset consisting of questions and corresponding answers was developed, with both question and answer generated by the gpt-4 model and based on a reference chunk.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/dataprep.png)Figure 1: From a large document (book), chunks were created, and for each chunk, a question and an answer were generated using gpt-4, where the answer is contained within the chunk.

Figure [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Data Preparation ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") shows the data preparation process. Initially, the dataset was break into chunks with <!-- MathML: <math alttext="1000" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S2.p2.m1"><semantics><mn>1000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1000</annotation></semantics></math> --> 10001000 tokens each, without overlapping, resulting in <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="140" id="S2.p2.m2"><semantics><mn>140</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">140</annotation></semantics></math> --> 140140 chunks. Then, using the prompt described in Appendix [A](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#A1 "Appendix A PROMPTS ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"), a <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="\{question,answer\}" id="S2.p2.m3"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{question,answer\}</annotation></semantics></math> --> {q​u​e​s​t​i​o​n,a​n​s​w​e​r}\{question,answer\} pair was created for each chunk in the style of the SQuAD dataset [[6](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib6 "")], meaning that the answer to the question is present within the reference text (chunk).

## 3 How to Evaluate

The contextual comparison of two text samples is not a straightforward task. For instance, despite the sentence<!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="{}_{1}=" display="inline" id="S3.p1.m1"><semantics><mrow><msub><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{1}=</annotation></semantics></math> --> 1={}_{1}= "Brazil has won 5 FIFA World Cup titles.", and sentence<!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="{}_{2}=" display="inline" id="S3.p1.m2"><semantics><mrow><msub><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{2}=</annotation></semantics></math> --> 2={}_{2}= "Brazil is the five-time champion of the FIFA World Cup." (both sentences translated into English for convenience) convey the same meaning, traditional metrics such as BLEU [[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib7 "")] and ROUGE [[8](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib8 "")] score may not be able to capture such similarity. Specifically, for the example cited:

- •     BLEU score <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="[\text{sentence}_{1},\text{sentence}_{2}]=0.33" display="inline" id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>sentence</mtext><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>sentence</mtext><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.33</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\text{sentence}_{1},\text{sentence}_{2}]=0.33</annotation></semantics></math> --> [sentence1,sentence2]=0.33[\text{sentence}_{1},\text{sentence}_{2}]=0.33

- •     ROUGE score <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="[\text{sentence}_{1},\text{sentence}_{2}]=0.22" id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>sentence</mtext><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>sentence</mtext><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.22</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\text{sentence}_{1},\text{sentence}_{2}]=0.22</annotation></semantics></math> --> [sentence1,sentence2]=0.22[\text{sentence}_{1},\text{sentence}_{2}]=0.22

Therefore, an approach widely used in the literature is to employ gpt-4 to provide a score based on a given prompt, a concept similar to what was done in the G-Eval work [[9](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib9 "")]. In this work, a scoring system divided into <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="5" display="inline" id="S3.p3.m1"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> --> 55 categories to compare two texts was devised, with scores defined as following (translated into English for convenience):

- •     score 1: The answer has no relation to the reference.

- •     score 3: The answer has little relevance but is not aligned with the reference.

- •     score 5: The answer has moderate relevance but contains inaccuracies.

- •     score 7: The answer is aligned with the reference but has minor omissions.

- •     score 10: The answer is completely accurate and aligns perfectly with the reference.

The prompt used in the evaluation is shown in Appendix [A](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#A1 "Appendix A PROMPTS ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"). Our approach uses a one-shot technique for each scoring category. Although, we believe that the evaluation could become more robust and deterministic with the addition of more few-shot examples for each scoring category, these possible variations were not explored in this work.

### 3.1 Relative Maximum Score

In order to assess performance variation for the followings experiments, we created a metric called the relative maximum score, which corresponds to the score given by a model when evaluating the correct combination of question and chunk for all pairs of a given dataset. Through this approach, it is possible to obtain the maximum score that an evaluated LLM could reach for a RAG system.

It’s worth noting that we did not explore prompt engineering techniques, although we are aware that prompt engineering has a direct impact on performance, as demonstrated in [[10](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib10 "")].

## 5 Advanced Experiments

The studies and experiments outlined in section [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S4 "4 Introductory Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") have shown unsatisfactory performance, marked by a degradation of at least <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="20\%" id="S5.p1.m1"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 20%20\% compared to the peak relative performance. Therefore, in this section, we explore various retrieval approaches for the RAG, recognizing that the quality of the retriever is a crucial factor in enhancing performance for this type of problem. We conducted an evaluation covering both sparse and dense search, a hybrid method, and even a multi-stage architecture using a reranker.

In pursuit of code debugging flexibility and easier customization at each stage, we chose not to utilize an RAG framework (like LangChain or Llama-Index). For a comprehensive guide on debugging RAG and more details about retrieval systems, refer to [[20](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib20 "")] and [[21](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib21 "")].

### 5.1 Retrievers

When deploying retrieval systems, it is essential to achieve a balance between “effectiveness” (How good are the results returned?) and “efficiency” (How much time it takes to return the results? or How much resources are used in terms of disk/RAM/GPU?). This balance ensures that latency, result quality, and computational budget remain within our application’s required limits. This work will exclusively focus on effectiveness measures to quantify the retrievers methods quality.

In our retriever experiments, the evaluation strategy centers around assessing how well the retriever performs in retrieving relevant information based on each given query <!-- MathML: <math alttext="q_{i}" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S5.SS1.p2.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> --> qiq_{i}. To achieve this, we employ the concept of recall. It is defined as the fraction of the relevant documents for a given query <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="q_{i}" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS1.p2.m2"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> --> qiq_{i} that are successfully retrieved in a ranked list <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="R" id="S5.SS1.p2.m3"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> --> RR [[21](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib21 "")]. This metric is based on binary relevance judgments, assuming that documents are either relevant or not [[21](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib21 "")]. In this paper, each chunk is considered a document and only the respective chunk <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="d_{i}" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS1.p2.m4"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> --> did_{i} is considered relevant to the query <!-- MathML: <math alttext="q_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS1.p2.m5"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> --> qiq_{i}. While recall is easy to interpret, it does not consider the specific rank positions in which the relevant chunk appears in <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="R" id="S5.SS1.p2.m6"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> --> RR.

To overcome this limitation, we introduce Reciprocal Rank (RR) into our analysis. In this metric, the rank of the first relevant document to the query in <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="R" display="inline" id="S5.SS1.p3.m1"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> --> RR is used to compute the RR score [[21](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib21 "")]. Therefore, Reciprocal Rank offers a more nuanced evaluation by assigning a higher value when the relevant chunk is returned in the early positions of our retrievers given the respective query.

Recall and Reciprocal Rank were evaluated at a specific cutoff so the measures are presented as R@k and MRR@k. For each query, its results are evaluated and their mean serves as an aggregated measure of effectiveness of a given retriever method. The retrievers are introduced below.

In the category of sparse retrievers, we emphasize the BM25, a technique grounded in statistical weighting to assess relevance between search terms and documents. BM25 employs a scoring function that takes into account term frequency and document length, offering an efficient approach for retrieving pertinent information and is typically used as a strong baseline. However, it is exact-match based and can be powerless when query and document are relevant to each other but has no common words.

On the other hand, when exploring dense retrievers, we often encounter approaches based on the called bi-encoder design [[22](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib22 "")]. The bi-encoder independently encodes queries and documents, creating separate vector representations before calculating similarity. An advantage of this approach is that it can be initialized ‘offline’: document embeddings can be precomputed, leaving only the query embedding being calculated at search time, reducing latency.

The hybrid search technique aims to leverage the best of both sparse and dense search approaches. Given a question, both searches are conducted in parallel, generating two lists of candidate documents to answer it. The challenge then lies in combining the two results in the best possible way, ensuring that the final hybrid list surpasses the individual searches. Essentially, we can conceptualize it as a voting system, where each searcher casts a vote on the relevance of a document to a given query, and in the end, the opinions are combined to produce a better result.

The multi-stage search architecture is based on the retrieve-and-rerank pipeline. In the first stage, a retriever with good recall is typically used to perform an initial filtering of the documents to be returned. From this narrowed-down list, these candidate documents are then sent to a second stage, which involves higher computational complexity, to rerank them and enhance the final effectiveness of the system.

Next, we provide more details about each retriever used.

#### 5.1.1 BM25

Due to the user-friendly nature of BM25, its inclusion as a retriever method is always a welcome addition in RAG evaluations. A study that aligns with the same reasoning, albeit for a different application, can be found in [[23](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib23 "")], which illustrates the benefits of employing this algorithm to establish a robust baseline. Given that our data shares similarities with the SQuAD dataset, it is expected that many words from the query would be present in the chunk, contributing to the favorable effectiveness of BM25.

In the BM25 ranking function, <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="k_{1}" id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p2.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> --> k1k_{1} and <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="b" display="inline" id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p2.m2"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> --> bb are parameters shaping term saturation and document length normalization, respectively. The BM25 formula integrates these parameters to score the relevance of a document to a query, offering flexibility in adjusting <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="k_{1}" id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p2.m3"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> --> k1k_{1} and <!-- MathML: <math alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p2.m4"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> --> bb for improving effectiveness in different retrieval scenarios.

Table 4: Comparison between BM25 packages using k1=0.82 and b=0.68.

Effectiveness is also influenced by chosen BM25 implementation. Pyserini’s BM25 implementation incorporates an analyzer with preprocessing steps such as stemming and language-specific stop word removal. For the sake of comparison, we included results obtained using rank-bm25 [[24](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib24 "")], a basic implementation without preprocessing that is widely used in Python and integrated into libraries like LangChain and Llama-index. The results can be seen in Table [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.1.1 BM25 ‣ 5.1 Retrievers ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator").

In this work, the Pyserini BM25 implementation [[25](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib25 "")] was used in all experiments considering <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="k_{1}" id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p4.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> --> k1k_{1}=0.82 and <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="b" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p4.m2"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> --> bb=0.68.

#### 5.1.2 ADA-002

OpenAI does not disclose extensive details about the ADA-002 architecture; however, we employed this model in retrieval as the presented bi-encoder design (Figure [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.1.2 ADA-002 ‣ 5.1 Retrievers ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator")): vector representations were constructed for all available chunks, and for each input query, its embedding was computed at search time. Subsequently, the similarity between the question and chunk were assessed using cosine similarity.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/bi_encoder.png)Figure 5: Bi-Encoder Architecture

Since we have no further details about ADA-002 we will refer to this approach only as dense retriever.

#### 5.1.3 Custom ADA-002

The Custom ADA-002 approach was also utilized in the dense retriever configuration presented in Section [5.1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.SS1.SSS2 "5.1.2 ADA-002 ‣ 5.1 Retrievers ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"). However, embedding customization played a key role in our attempt to enhance the overall representation.

Embedding customization is not limited solely to OpenAI’s embeddings; it is a technique applicable to other embeddings of the same kind. There is a significant variety of approaches to optimize a matrix, with one of them being the application of Multiple Negative Ranking Loss, as presented in the article "Efficient Natural Language Response Suggestion for Smart Reply," Section 4.4 [[26](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib26 "")]. However, given our current focus on simplicity, we will reserve the exploration of this technique for future work. At this moment, we choose to utilize the Mean Squared Error (MSE) Loss.

For the fine-tuning stage, it is necessary to have two types of samples:

#### 5.1.5 Reranker

The fundamental idea underlying multi-stage ranking is to divide document ranking into a sequence of stages. After an initial retrieval, which usually involves a sparse retriever or dense retriever, each subsequent stage re-evaluates and reranks the set of candidates forwarded from the preceding stage. Figure [9](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 5.1.5 Reranker ‣ 5.1 Retrievers ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") represents a multi-stage pipeline where Pyserini BM25 performs the first stage and the candidate chunks are then re-evaluated by the reranker. After that, the final reranked list called retrieved chunks is presented as final result formed by <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="k" id="S5.SS1.SSS5.p1.m1"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> --> kk chunks.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/reranker.png)Figure 9: Reranker Pipeline

Transformers-based models are commonly employed as rerankers, leveraging their capability to enhance the effectiveness of information retrieval systems by capturing intricate relationships and contextual information within documents and queries.

The initial utilization of transformers within a multi-stage ranking framework was presented in the study [[28](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib28 "")]. Their proposed model, known as monoBERT, transforms the ranking process into a relevance classification problem. It achieves this by sorting texts based on the conditional probability <!-- MathML: <math alttext="P(\text{Relevant}=1\,|\,d_{i};q)" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS1.SSS5.p3.m1"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>Relevant</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0.170em">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(\text{Relevant}=1\,|\,d_{i};q)</annotation></semantics></math> --> P⁡(Relevant=1|di;q)P(\text{Relevant}=1\,|\,d_{i};q), where <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="q" display="inline" id="S5.SS1.SSS5.p3.m2"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> --> qq is the query and <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d_{i}" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S5.SS1.SSS5.p3.m3"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> --> did_{i} represents documents [[21](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib21 "")]. The model simultaneously processes both queries and documents. This simultaneous processing leads to a more enriched interaction between them, often resulting in improved effectiveness [[29](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib29 "")], [[30](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib30 "")]. However, this neural models have a substantial number of parameters and the scoring of query-document pairs occurs at inference time. This, in turn, increases computational costs and latency. This kind of model is also known by cross-encoder. Refer to Figure [10](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 5.1.5 Reranker ‣ 5.1 Retrievers ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") for an illustration of the query-document pair processing.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/cross_encoder.png)Figure 10: Cross-Encoder

In the other hand, monoT5 is a sequence-to-sequence reranker [[31](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib31 "")] that uses T5 models [[32](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib32 "")] to generate relevance scores between a pair of query and document. T5 models treat all tasks as text-to-text, requiring some adaptations for the query/document similarity task. During training, the format 'Query: {query} Document: {document} Relevant:' is used, with labels yes if the document is relevant to the query, and no otherwise. At inference time, the same format as the training data is used to format pairs of queries and documents to feed the model, and a single-token greedy decode is performed. The score is then obtained by calculating the softmax value considering only the tokens no and yes, and selecting the value corresponding to the yes token. Note that the tokens no and yes are the tokens used in the version provided by [[33](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib33 "")], but the publication that introduced the monoT5 architecture, [[31](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib31 "")], uses the tokens false and true. Figure [11](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 5.1.5 Reranker ‣ 5.1 Retrievers ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") contains an illustration of the monoT5 architecture’s inference process.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/monot5.png)Figure 11: monoT5’s inference process

In our experiments, Pyserini BM25 was employed as first-stage retrieval, retrieving 50 documents to be reranked in the second stage. In the second stage, we utilized the model unicamp-dl/mt5-base-en-pt-msmarco-v2, a sequence-to-sequence reranker trained on pairs of queries and documents in English and Portuguese from the dataset [[33](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib33 "")].

## 6 Conclusions

The implementation of RAG systems faces challenges such as the effective integration of retrieval models, efficient representation learning, the diversity of data, the optimization of computational efficiency, evaluation, and text generation quality. Faced with these constantly evolving obstacles, this article proposes best practices for the implementation, optimization, and evaluation of RAG on a Brazilian Portuguese dataset, focusing on a simplified pipeline for inference and experimentation.

So far, we have introduced the main components and methods along with their results and gaps. In this section, we will discuss key points that contribute to the performance improvement in RAG applications. We will start by discussing the relationship between the quality of the retriever and the achieved performance, in which our approach showed a significant improvement of MRR@10 by <!-- MathML: <math alttext="35.4\%" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S6.p2.m1"><semantics><mrow><mn>35.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">35.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 35.4%35.4\% compared to the baseline. Next, we will address the impact of input size on performance. In this domain, we observed that it is possible to enhance the best information retrieval strategy by <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="2.4\%" id="S6.p2.m2"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 2.4%2.4\% through input size optimization. Finally, we will present the complete architecture of RAG with our recommendations. When evaluating the final accuracy of our approach, we reached <!-- MathML: <math alttext="98.61\%" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S6.p2.m3"><semantics><mrow><mn>98.61</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">98.61\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 98.61%98.61\%, representing an improvement of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="40.73" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S6.p2.m4"><semantics><mn>40.73</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40.73</annotation></semantics></math> --> 40.7340.73 in less degradation score compared to the baseline.

Despite achieving perfect recall for <!-- MathML: <math alttext="9" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S6.SS2.p2.m1"><semantics><mn>9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9</annotation></semantics></math> --> 99 chunks, as evidenced in Table [6](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.2 Retrievers Results ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"), using an input with <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="9000" id="S6.SS2.p2.m2"><semantics><mn>9000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9000</annotation></semantics></math> --> 90009000 tokens, <!-- MathML: <math alttext="6000" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S6.SS2.p2.m3"><semantics><mn>6000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6000</annotation></semantics></math> --> 60006000 more than the best scenario (<!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="3" id="S6.SS2.p2.m4"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math> --> 33 chunks), did not result in the best performance. As discussed in Section [4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S4.SS2 "4.2 Long Context ‣ 4 Introductory Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"), the quality of RAG is directly related to the input size and the position where the answer is located. Therefore, the final results confirm the observations made in our experiments.

Moreover, from a cost perspective, it is crucial to avoid overloading the LLM with a large number of input tokens, as the cost is also based on the amount of input text.

It is important to note that the results obtained in this study cannot be considered as a generalization for other datasets. Exploratory Data Analysis and the use of good retriever practices, as presented in [[34](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib34 "")], are always a solid path to achieving good results.

### 6.3 Final Results

Despite this work being grounded in a single dataset, it is always crucial to emphasize the importance of data quality. In a simplified manner, as illustrated in Figure [13](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S6.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ 6.3 Final Results ‣ 6 Conclusions ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"), data quality in RAG can be divided into Input, Retriever, and Evaluation.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/core_points_RAG.png)Figure 13: Core Points in RAG.

- •     Input: How are the queries formulated? Are they synthetic or generic? What is the application’s purpose? Building a RAG for a chatbot differs significantly from constructing a RAG for extracting information from a long and complex document.

- •     Retriever: How do the data behave in information retrieval? Are the queries strongly linked by keywords in the text? What is the cosine similarity of query-to-query, query-to-document, and document-to-document?

- •     Evaluation: How are the data measured? Defining metrics and success rates, as in the first experiment, is always a safe path to avoid biases. Build the evaluation system before testing, avoiding bias.

In conclusion, the main contribution of this work was to identify and present the best possible configuration of techniques and parameters for a RAG application. Figure [14](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S6.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ 6.3 Final Results ‣ 6 Conclusions ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") provides a summarized overview of the end-to-end experiment results for the discussed approaches, and the best practices recommended by this study achieve a final accuracy of <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="98.61\%" display="inline" id="S6.SS3.p3.m1"><semantics><mrow><mn>98.61</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">98.61\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 98.61%98.61\%, representing an improvement of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="40.73" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S6.SS3.p3.m2"><semantics><mn>40.73</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40.73</annotation></semantics></math> --> 40.7340.73 percentage points compared to the baseline.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/final_results.png)Figure 14: RAG Performance: Performance evolution on the Harry Potter dataset, where an accuracy of 100% is considered the relative maximum.

### 6.4 Future Work

We will expand our search to cover additional data sets, preferably those containing real data that already have questions and the reference documents for the answers. By using such datasets, we intend to explore techniques related to segmentation and chunk construction, as elaborated in Appendix B, Section [B](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#A2 "Appendix B Sentence Window ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator").

## Appendix B Sentence Window

There are a wide variety of techniques available for dealing with RAG and new approaches are constantly emerging. In this work we highlight the main existing strategies, although we have also explored others, such as the RAG Sentence Window approach.

The sentence window chunk constitutes a strategy embedded in the llama-index11 1 <https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/examples/node_postprocessor/MetadataReplacementDemo.html>, which employs the small-to-large approach. The entire chunk retrieval process is based on cosine similarity. Initially, a single sentence is retrieved, followed by expanding (window) around the retrieved sentence to construct a more extensive chunk. This method implies that the most relevant context is always centered and retrieved first, as opposed to being at the edges of a chunk boundary. Figure [15](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#A2.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ Appendix B Sentence Window ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") illustrates the comparison between naive chunks and those obtained through the "sentence window" strategy.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/sentence-window_chunk_2.png)Figure 15: Comparison between the naive chunking and small to big strategies, where the latter initially retrieves a single sentence and then performs windowing with padding on both sides.

Despite being a promising technique, the results on our dataset were inferior to the naive strategy, as indicated in Table [9](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#A2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix B Sentence Window ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator").

Table 9: Performance of the RAG Sentence Window.

Our hypothesis for the low performance includes:

1. 1.     The construction of the question and answer occurred after the "chunk" cut, so there is no answer between two chunks.

2. 2.     Embedding sentence by sentence in the Harry Potter book causes ambiguity: there are multiple sentences with the name Harry Potter, which adds a significant challenge to the step of retrieving the correct sentence.

The **United States secretary of energy** is the head of the [United States Department of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy "United States Department of Energy"), a member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") and fifteenth in the [presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession"). The position was created on October 1, 1977, when President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") signed the [Department of Energy Organization Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Energy_Organization_Act "Department of Energy Organization Act"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-2) establishing the department. Originally, the secretary and the department focused on energy production and regulation. Over time, the emphasis shifted to developing technology for more efficient energy sources and energy education. After the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"), the department's attention also turned to [radioactive waste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_waste "Radioactive waste") disposal and environmental quality maintenance.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-3)

Former [secretary of defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Defense "United States Secretary of Defense") [James Schlesinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_R._Schlesinger "James R. Schlesinger") was the first secretary of energy. As a Republican nominated by Democratic president Jimmy Carter, Schlesinger’s appointment remains the only instance of a president choosing a member of another political party for the position. Schlesinger is also the only secretary to be dismissed from the post.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-4) [Hazel O'Leary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazel_R._O'Leary "Hazel R. O'Leary"), [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton")’s first secretary of energy, was the first female and first African American to hold the position.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-5) The first [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans "Hispanic and Latino Americans") to serve as energy secretary was Clinton’s second energy secretary, [Federico Peña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Peña "Federico Peña"). [Spencer Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Abraham "Spencer Abraham") became the first [Arab American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Americans "Arab Americans") to hold the position on January 20, 2001, under President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"). [Steven Chu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Chu "Steven Chu"), appointed on January 20, 2009, under President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), became the first [Asian American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Americans "Asian Americans") to hold the position. Chu also served as the longest-serving secretary of energy and was the first individual to join the Cabinet after having received a Nobel Prize.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-6) Former Michigan governor, [Jennifer Granholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Granholm "Jennifer Granholm"), confirmed on February 25, 2021 under President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"), was the second woman to lead the Department of Energy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-7) [Chris Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Wright "Chris Wright") is the current secretary of energy under the Trump administration, confirmed on February, 3, 2025.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-8)

## Nuclear weapons

In addition to responsibilities related to generation and use of energy, the secretary is the most senior official other than the president of the United States or secretary of defense with primary responsibility for the nation's approximately 3,800 viable nuclear weapons. This arrangement is intended to maintain full civilian control over strategic weapons, except as directed by the president for specific military uses.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-9) The department of energy is responsible for the building, maintenance, and disposal of all nuclear weapons within the United States' arsenal in addition to safeguarding these weapons when they are not actively deployed in military service.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-10) Under the terms of several successive treaties, most recently New START, the United States has reduced its strategic arsenal to 1,500 deployed weapons. Consequently, many older legacy weapons systems have been dismantled or scheduled for dismantlement, with their core radioactive fuel - generally plutonium - being reprocessed into reactor-grade or space exploration fuel.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-11)

# Secretaries of Energy

### Former Secretaries of Energy

![portrait of DAN BROUILLETTE](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/2026-05/DAN_BROUILLETTE_PORTRAITV3_0.jpg?itok=QazG7XqZ)

**Dan Brouillette**  
Born: August 18, 1962, Paincourtville, Louisiana  
Nominated: November 7, 2019  
Confirmed: December 2, 2019  
Term of Office: December 11, 2019 – January 20, 2021  
President: Donald Trump  
B.S., University of Maryland. Chief of Staff for Representative Billy Tauzin of Louisiana, 1989-1997. Assistant Secretary of Energy for Congressional and Intergovernmental Affairs, 2001-2003. Staff director for the House Energy and Commerce Committee, 2003-2004. Deputy Secretary of Energy, 2017-19.

![Photograph of Secretary of Energy Rick Perry](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/2017/06/f34/PERRY_FINAL_PORTRAIT_KSS3248_0.jpg?itok=THlt4iha)

**Rick Perry**  
Born: March 4, 1950, Haskell, Texas  
Nominated: December 14, 2016  
Confirmed: March 2, 2017  
Term of Office: March 2, 2017 – December 1, 2019  
President: Donald Trump  
B.S., Texas A&M University, 1972. Texas House of Representatives, 64th District, 1985-1991. Agriculture Commissioner of Texas, 1991-1999. Lieutenant Governor of Texas, 1999-2000. Governor of Texas, 2000-2015.

.

![Secretary Ernest Moniz](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/moniz_2_0.jpg?itok=17xGDPn_)

**Ernest Moniz**  
Born: December 22, 1944, Fall River, Massachusetts  
Nominated: March 4, 2013  
Confirmed: May 16, 2013  
Term of Office: May 21, 2013 - January 20, 2017  
President: Barack Obama  
B.S., Boston College, 1966. Ph.D., Stanford University, 1972. Professor of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), 1973-2013. Associate Director for Science, Office of Science and Technology Policy, 1995-1997. Under Secretary, Department of Energy, 1997-2001. Director, MIT Energy Initiative, 2006-2013.

![Secretary Steven Chu](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/timelines/Steven%20Chu_0.jpg?itok=rg-339AG)

**Steven Chu**  
Born: February 28, 1948, St. Louis, Missouri  
Nominated: December 15, 2008  
Confirmed: January 20, 2009  
Term of Office: January 21, 2009 - April 22, 2013  
President: Barack Obama  
A.B. and B.S., University of Rochester, 1970. Ph.D., U.C. Berkeley, 1976. Postdoctoral Fellow, U.C. Berkeley, 1976-1978. Member, Technical Staff, AT&T, 1978-83. Head of Quantum Electronic Dept., AT&T Bell Laboratories, 1983-87. Professor of Physics and Applied Physics, Stanford University, 1987-2008. Co-recipient of the Nobel Prize for Physics, 1997. Director, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, 2004-2009

![Secretary Samuel W. Bodman](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/migrated/nnsa/2017/11/f39/71-Bodman_0.jpg?itok=TTGn17MP)

**Samuel W. Bodman**  
Born: November 26, 1938, Chicago, Illinois  
Nominated: December 10, 2004  
Confirmed: January 31, 2005  
Term of Office: February 2005 - January 2009

![Secretary Spencer Abraham](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/timelines/Spencer%20Abraham_0.jpg?itok=aPqMimoT)

**Spencer Abraham**  
Born: June 12, 1952, Lansing, Michigan  
Nominated: January 3, 2001  
Confirmed: January 20, 2001  
Term of Office: January 20, 2001 - January 31, 2005  
President: George Bush  
B.A. Political Science, Michigan State University, 1974. J.D., Harvard University, 1979. Chairman, Michigan Republican Party, 1982-1990. Deputy Chief of Staff, Office of the Vice President, 1990-1991. Co-Chairman, National Republican Congressional Committee, 1991-1993. U. S. Senator, 1995-2001.

![Secretary Bill Richardson](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/timelines/Bill%20Richardson_0.jpg?itok=4qUGa0Ar)

**Bill Richardson**  
Born: November 15, 1947, Pasadena, California  
Nominated: July 22, 1998  
Confirmed: July 31, 1998  
Term of Office: August 18, 1998-January 20, 2001  
President: Bill Clinton  
M.A., The Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy, 1971. U.S. Congressman from New Mexico, 1983-97. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations, 1997-98.

![Secretary Federico Peña](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/timelines/Federico%20Pena%20Oval_0.jpg?itok=vL_up0LJ)

**Federico Peña**  
Born: March 15, 1947, Laredo, Texas  
Nominated: December 19, 1996  
Confirmed: March 12, 1997  
Term of Office: March 12, 1997-June 30, 1998  
President: Bill Clinton  
J.D., University of Texas, 1972. Mayor, City and County of Denver, 1983-91. Secretary of Transportation, 1993-97.

![Secretary Hazel R. O'Leary](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/timelines/Hazel%20O%27Leary_0_0.jpg?itok=sa92vQ4S)

**Hazel R. O'Leary**  
Born: May 17, 1937, Newport News, Virginia  
Nominated: January 20, 1993  
Confirmed: January 21, 1993  
Term of Office: January 22, 1993-January 20, 1997  
President: Bill Clinton  
B.A., Fisk University, 1959. J.D., Rutgers University, 1966. Assistant Attorney General, State of New Jersey, 1967-68. Administrator, Economic Regulatory Administration, 1979-80. Vice President and then President, Northern States Power Company, 1989-93.

![Secretary James Watkins](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/timelines/James%20Watkins_0.jpg?itok=chH-jpul)

**Admiral James Watkins**  
Born: March 7, 1927, Alhambra, California  
Deceased: July 26, 2012  
Nominated: January 20, 1989  
Confirmed: March 1, 1989  
Term of Office: March 1, 1989-January 20, 1993  
President: George Bush  
B.S., United States Naval Academy. Graduate, reactor engineering course, Oak Ridge National Laboratory. M.S., Naval Postgraduate School, 1958. Chief of Naval Operations, 1982-86. Chairman, Presidential Commission on the Human Immunodeficiency Virus Epidemic, 1987-88.

![Secretary John S. Herrington](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/timelines/John%20Herrington%20Oval_0.jpg?itok=BApZ9LiS)

**John S. Herrington**  
Born: May 31, 1939, Los Angeles, California  
Nominated: January 18, 1985  
Confirmed: February 6, 1985  
Term of Office: February 7, 1985-January 20, 1989  
President: Ronald Reagan  
J.D., University of California, Hastings College of Law, 1964. Assistant Secretary of the Navy, 1981-83. Assistant to the President of the United States, 1984.

![Secretary Donald P. Hodel](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/migrated/nnsa/2017/11/f39/33-Hodel_0.jpg?itok=43EQknBK)

**Donald P. Hodel**  
Born: May 23, 1935, Portland, Oregon  
Appointment: November 5, 1982  
Confirmed: December 8, 1982  
Term of Office: November 5, 1982-February 7, 1985  
President: Ronald Reagan  
B.A. Government, Harvard University, 1957. J.D., Oregon School of Law, 1960. Administrator, Bonneville Power Administration, 1972-77. Under Secretary of the Interior, 1981-82.

![Secretary James B. Edwards](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/migrated/nnsa/2017/11/f39/31-James_B__Edwards_0.jpg?itok=PtstDWxA)

**James B. Edwards**  
Born: June 24, 1927, Hawthorne, Florida  
Nominated: January 20, 1981  
Confirmed: January 22, 1981  
Term of Office: January 23, 1981-November 5, 1982  
President: Ronald Reagan  
DMD, University of Louisville, 1955. Governor of South Carolina, 1975-79.

![Secretary Charles Duncan](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/migrated/nnsa/2017/11/f39/Secretary-Duncan-Portrait_0.jpg?itok=ch3m6Cw2)

**Charles Duncan**  
Born: September 9, 1926, Houston, Texas  
Nominated: July 20, 1979  
Confirmed: July 31, 1979  
Term of Office: August 24, 1979-January 20, 1981  
President: Jimmy Carter  
B.S. Chemical Engineering, Rice University, 1947. President, Coca-Cola Company, 1971-74. Deputy Secretary of Defense, 1977-79.

![Secretary James Schlesinger](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/2019/11/f68/Schlesinger%20black%20and%20white_0.jpg?itok=maz4RpUl)

**James Schlesinger**  
Born: February 15, 1929, New York City  
Confirmed: August 4, 1977  
Term of Office: August 6, 1977-August 23, 1979  
President: Jimmy Carter  
Ph.D., Harvard, 1956. Chairman, Atomic Energy Commission, 1971-73. Director, Central Intelligence Agency, 1973. Secretary of Defense, 1973-75. Assistant to President Carter, 1977.

**Danny Ray Brouillette**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-1) ([/bruːˈjɛt/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") born August 18, 1962) is an American government official, lobbyist, businessman, and [Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Army "US Army") veteran who served as the 15th [United States Secretary of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy "United States Secretary of Energy") in the [first Donald Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump") from 2019 to 2021.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-2) He previously served as the [United States Deputy Secretary of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Energy "United States Deputy Secretary of Energy") from August 2017 to December 2019. In 2023, Brouillette was named president and chief executive officer elect of the [Edison Electric Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edison_Electric_Institute "Edison Electric Institute").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-3)

## Early life and career

Danny Ray Brouillette was born on August 18, 1962, in [Paincourtville, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paincourtville,_Louisiana "Paincourtville, Louisiana"). He graduated from the [University of Maryland Global Campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland_Global_Campus "University of Maryland Global Campus") in 1995.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-:1-4)

Following his service in the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army"), Brouillette was U.S. representative [Billy Tauzin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Tauzin "Billy Tauzin")'s legislative director from 1989 to 1997.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-:1-4) From 1997 to 2000, he was Senior Vice President of R. Duffy Wall & Associates,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-5) a DC-based lobbying firm.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-6) Brouillette was Assistant Secretary for Congressional and Intergovernmental Affairs in the [United States Department of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy "United States Department of Energy") from 2001 to 2003 under President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-:0-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-8)

He was chief of staff under Rep. Billy Tauzin and was also staff director for the [United States House Committee on Energy and Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_Energy_and_Commerce "United States House Committee on Energy and Commerce") from 2003 to 2004, when Tauzin chaired the committee.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-:2-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-:3-10) Brouillette was involved in crafting provisions included in the [Energy Policy Act of 2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_Policy_Act_of_2005 "Energy Policy Act of 2005"), specifically with respect to the Department of Energy loan guarantee program and federal authorization of importation and exportation of liquid natural gas.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-:2-9)

From 2004 to 2006, Brouillette was a vice president at [Ford Motor Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Motor_Company "Ford Motor Company") and sat on Ford's North American Operating Committee.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-:2-9) In 2006, Brouillette became head of public policy and senior vice president at [United Services Automobile Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USAA "USAA").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-11)

Brouillette was a member of Louisiana's State Mineral and Energy Board from 2013 to 2016.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-:3-10) He was awarded the 2020 Distinguished Alumnus Award by the [University of Maryland Global Campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland_Global_Campus "University of Maryland Global Campus") [Alumni Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alumni_association "Alumni association").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-12) In 2021, he joined the [American Council for Capital Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Council_for_Capital_Formation "American Council for Capital Formation")'s board of advisors.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-14)

### Deputy Secretary of Energy (2017–2019)

On April 3, 2017, President Donald Trump announced he would nominate Brouillette as [United States Deputy Secretary of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Energy "United States Deputy Secretary of Energy") in the United States Department of Energy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-:0-7) Brouillette was confirmed by the U.S. Senate on August 3, 2017. He was sworn in as the Deputy Secretary of Energy on August 8, 2017.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-15)

### Secretary of Energy (2019–2021)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Dan_Brouillette_sworn_in_as_Secretary_of_Energy.jpg/250px-Dan_Brouillette_sworn_in_as_Secretary_of_Energy.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dan_Brouillette_sworn_in_as_Secretary_of_Energy.jpg)Dan Brouillette being sworn in on December 11, 2019.

On October 18, 2019, President Trump announced he would nominate Brouillette as [United States Secretary of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy "United States Secretary of Energy") to replace [Rick Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Perry "Rick Perry"), who had announced he would step down by the end of the year.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-trumptweetnom-16) On November 7, 2019, President Trump sent his nomination to the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-17)

Perry formally resigned as Energy Secretary on December 1, 2019, making Brouillette the acting secretary, as his nomination was still pending before the U.S. Senate. On December 2, 2019, the Senate confirmed his nomination by a vote of 70–15.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-18) Brouillette was formally sworn in on December 11, 2019.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-19) Then-Under Secretary of Energy [Mark Menezes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Menezes "Mark Menezes") served as Acting Deputy Secretary of Energy until he was confirmed as Deputy Secretary on August 4, 2020.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-20)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Secretary_Dan_Brouillette.jpg/250px-Secretary_Dan_Brouillette.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Secretary_Dan_Brouillette.jpg)Secretary Brouillette speaks at a farewell event at the Department of Energy Headquarters in [Washington D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") in January 2021.

In December 2020, as part of the recently signed [Abraham Accords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Accords "Abraham Accords"), Brouillette convened a "first-of-its kind" meeting between the energy minister of Israel and counterparts from several Arab nations.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-21)

On January 7, 2021, Brouillette promised a seamless handover between the [Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump") and [Biden administrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden_administration "Biden administration").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-22)

## Post-Trump administration

### Sempra Infrastructure

Brouillette was named the president of [Sempra Infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sempra "Sempra") in July 2021 and started with the company in November of that year.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-23) During his time with Sempra, Brouillette oversaw the Port Arthur [LNG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquefied_natural_gas "Liquefied natural gas") project in Texas[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-24) and a heads of agreement deal with TotalEnergies, Mitsui, Mitsubishi and NYK for Cameron LNG Phase 2.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-25)

### Edison Electric Institute

On August 16, 2023, the [Edison Electric Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edison_Electric_Institute "Edison Electric Institute"), the [interest group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advocacy_group "Advocacy group") for United States [investor-owned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investor-owned_utilities_in_the_United_States "Investor-owned utilities in the United States") [electric utilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_utility "Electric utility"), named Brouillette its president and chief executive officer, effective January 1, 2024.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-26) He resigned on October 28, 2024, less than 10 months after taking the position, saying he wanted to focus on global energy issues.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-27)

## Personal life

Brouillette and his wife, Adrienne, are U.S. Army veterans and the parents of nine children, all of whom the couple homeschooled.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-28) They reside in [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Brouillette#cite_note-:0-7) He served in the Army from 1982 to 1987 as a tank commander in Germany in the "[Fulda Gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulda_Gap "Fulda Gap")" and as a [Drill Sergeant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drill_instructor#United_States "Drill instructor") in the [Army Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Reserve "United States Army Reserve") in South Carolina.

pergunta: Can you make a report about all the remembrance bosses of elden ring, considering both the base game and the DLC. I want to know all the rewards that can be traded for each remembrance boss.
resposta:
# Remembrance Bosses in Elden Ring: Complete Guide to Tradeable Rewards

## Overview
In *Elden Ring*, **Remembrances** are powerful items that can be obtained by defeating specific bosses using the Remembrance mechanic. Each Remembrance boss drops **two unique tradeable items** (options) that can be acquired by trading the Remembrance to **Finger Reader Enia**. This report covers all Remembrance bosses from the base game and the *Shadow of the Erdtree* DLC, along with their respective tradeable rewards.

---

## Base Game Remembrance Bosses (15)

| Remembrance | Boss | Reward Option 1 | Reward Option 2 | Rune Value |
|-------------|------|-----------------|-----------------|------------|
| **Remembrance of the Grafted** | Godrick the Grafted | Axe of Godrick (weapon) | Grafted Dragon (weapon) | 20,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Full Moon Queen** | Rennala, Queen of the Full Moon | Rennala’s Full Moon (sorcery) | Carian Regal Scepter (weapon) | 20,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Starscourge** | Starscourge Radahn | Starscourge Greatsword (weapon) | Lion Greatbow (weapon) | 40,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Regal Ancestor** | Regal Ancestor Spirit | Winged Greathorn (greataxe) | Ancestral Spirit’s Horn (talisman) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Omen King** | Morgott the Omen King | Morgott’s Cursed Sword (weapon) | Regal Omen Bairn (tool) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Naturalborn** | Astel, Naturalborn of the Void | Bastard’s Stars (weapon) | Bloodboon (incantation) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Blasphemous** | Rykard, Lord of Blasphemy | Rykard’s Rancor (sorcery) | Blasphemous Blade (weapon) | 50,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Lichdragon** | Lichdragon Fortissax | Fortissax’s Lightning Spear (incantation) | Death Lightning (incantation) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Fire Giant** | Fire Giant | Giant’s Red Braid (weapon) | Burn O Flame! (incantation) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Blood Lord** | Mohg, Lord of Blood | Mohgwyn’s Sacred Spear (weapon) | Bloodboon (incantation) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Black Blade** | Maliketh, the Black Blade | Maliketh’s Black Blade (weapon) | Black Blade (incantation) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Dragonlord** | Dragonlord Placidusax | Dragon King’s Cragblade (weapon) | Placidusax’s Ruin (incantation) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of Hoarah Loux** | Hoarah Loux, Warrior | Axe of Godfrey (weapon) | Ash of War: Hoarah Loux’s Earthshaker (ash of war) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Rot Goddess** | Malenia, Blade of Miquella | Hand of Malenia (weapon) | Scarlet Aeonia (incantation) | 50,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Elden Beast** | Elden Beast | Elden Remembrance (item) | Sacred Relic Sword (weapon) | 50,000 |

*Sources: Elden Ring Wiki (Fextralife) – Remembrances table.*

---

## Shadow of the Erdtree DLC Remembrance Bosses (10–11)

| Remembrance | Boss | Reward Option 1 | Reward Option 2 | Rune Value |
|-------------|------|-----------------|-----------------|------------|
| **Remembrance of the Dancing Lion** | Divine Beast Dancing Lion | Enraged Divine Beast (talisman) | Ash of War: Divine Beast Frost Stomp (ash of war) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Twin Moon Knight** | Rellana, Twin Moon Knight | Rellana’s Twin Blades (weapon) | Rellana’s Twin Moons (sorcery) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Putrescent Knight** | Putrescent Knight | Putrescence Cleaver (weapon) | Vortex of Putrescence (incantation) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Wild Boar Rider** | Commander Gaius | Sword Lance (weapon) | Blades of Stone (sorcery) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Shadow Sunflower** | Scadutree Avatar | Shadow Sunflower Blossom (colossal weapon) | Land of Shadow (incantation) | 40,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Impaler** (Messmer) | Messmer the Impaler | Spear of the Impaler (weapon) | Messmer’s Orb (incantation) | 40,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Saint of the Bud** | Romina, Saint of the Bud | Poleblade of the Bud (weapon) | Rotten Butterflies (incantation) | 30,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Mother of Fingers** | Metyr, Mother of Fingers | Staff of the Great Beyond (weapon) | Gazing Finger (colossal weapon) | 40,000 |
| **Remembrance of the Lord of Frenzied Flame** | Midra, Lord of Frenzied Flame | Greatsword of Damnation (weapon) | Midra’s Flame of Frenzy (incantation) | 40,000 |
| **Remembrance of a God and a Lord** | Radahn, Consort of Miquella | Greatsword of Radahn (Lord) (weapon) | Greatsword of Radahn (Light) (weapon) | 50,000 |
| **Heart of Bayle** (key item) | Bayle The Dread | Bayle’s Flame Lightning (incantation) | Bayle’s Tyranny (incantation) | N/A |

*Note: Heart of Bayle is a special key item that functions similarly to a Remembrance but is not a boss. It is included here as a DLC Remembrance-like item.*

*Sources: Elden Ring Wiki (Fextralife) – Shadow of the Erdtree Remembrances table; Fandom wiki – Remembrance Bosses.*

---

## Summary of Tradeable Rewards

Each Remembrance boss offers two distinct tradeable items (options). The rewards span multiple categories:

- **Weapons** (most common): Axe of Godrick, Carian Regal Scepter, Starscourge Greatsword, Dragon King’s Cragblade, etc.
- **Talismans**: Ancestral Spirit’s Horn, Enraged Divine Beast, etc.
- **Sorceries**: Rennala’s Full Moon, Rellana’s Twin Moons, etc.
- **Incantations**: Bloodboon, Messmer’s Orb, Rotten Butterflies, etc.
- **Ash of War**: Ash of War: Hoarah Loux’s Earthshaker, Ash of War: Divine Beast Frost Stomp.
- **Colossal Weapons**: Shadow Sunflower Blossom, Gazing Finger.
- **Tools**: Regal Omen Bairn.

All items are fully tradeable for Rune at any merchant and can be used to enhance your build, unlock spells, or equip your character.

---

## How to Obtain These Rewards

1. **Locate the boss** in the world (see locations in the tables).
2. **Defeat the boss** (defeating it grants the Remembrance item itself).
3. **Trade the Remembrance to Finger Reader Enia** at any Wandering Mausoleum or Remembrance Duplication Coffin to receive one of the two tradeable options.

---

## Conclusion

*Elden Ring* features **25 Remembrances** in total (15 from the base game, 10–11 from *Shadow of the Erdtree*), each providing two unique tradeable rewards. Whether you seek powerful weapons, magical talismans, or incantations, the Remembrance system offers a diverse array of items that can be traded for Rune or directly equipped. Mastering these bosses unlocks valuable gear that can significantly aid your journey through the Lands Between.

*Report compiled from the Elden Ring Wiki (Fextralife) and Fandom’s Remembrance Bosses page.*

Remembrance of the Dancing Lion, hewn into the Scadutree. The power of its namesake can be unlocked by the Finger Reader. Alternatively, it can be used to gain a great bounty of runes. When the Impaler's army assailed the tower, the ritual of the lion dance was turned toward martial ends—its divinity, its fury, its light-footed beauty.

Remembrance of Rellana, the Twin Moon Knight, hewn into the Scadutree. The power of its namesake can be unlocked by the Finger Reader. Alternatively, it can be used to gain a great bounty of runes. Once a Carian princess, Rellana disavowed her birthright and chose to stand at Messmer's side instead, knowing full well that not even the brilliance of the moon could grant him succor. Before long, she became known as the Sword of Messmer.

All tainted flesh eventually becomes putrescence, and this clump of it imbibed St. Trina's nectar, which granted it eternal rest. And so it was that putrescence became her knight.

Both were as elder brothers to the lion, and both were cursed from birth. In spite of, or perhaps because of this very reason, Gaius was both Messmer's friend and the leader of his men.

The Scadutree is the shadow of the Erdtree. Born of dark notions that bear no sense of Order, that twist and bend its stock, rendering it brittle.

Remembrance of Messmer the Impaler, hewn into the Scadutree. The power of its namesake can be unlocked by the Finger Reader. Alternatively, it can be used to gain a great bounty of runes. A malevolent snake writhed within Messmer, and so his very mother plucked out his eye and put in its place a seal of grace. Yet, having done so, her fear compelled her to secret away her child within the realm of shadow. Hidden away—keeping company with the original sin, and a hatred that would not be confined.

Perhaps then, the buds might find somewhere to gain purchase once more, within the scorched remains.

As the golden barbs inflicted eternal agony upon him, Midra held fast to Nanaya's entreaty: "Endure." The word was a curse.

The biatrial heart of Bayle the Dread. Dotted with horn-like gravel stones and glistening with deep-red liquor. Gorge upon this at the Grand Altar of Dragon Communion to absorb Bayle's power. The purest form of Communion, in the words of its priestess. Only one reward may be selected per playthrough.

#### [remembrance of a god and a lord](https://eldenring.wiki.fextralife.com/Remembrance_of_a_God_and_a_Lord "Remembrance of a God and a Lord")  [Remembrance of a God and a Lord](https://eldenring.wiki.fextralife.com/Remembrance_of_a_God_and_a_Lord "Remembrance of a God and a Lord")  [sote new](https://eldenring.wiki.fextralife.com/File:Sote-new.png)

Remembrance of Radahn, consort of Miquella, hewn into the Scadutree. The power of its namesake can be unlocked by the Finger Reader. Alternatively, it can be used to gain a great bounty of runes. In their childhood, Miquella saw in Radahn a lord. His strength, and his kindness, that stood in stark contrast with their afflicted selves. And so Miquella made his heartfelt wish. That Radahn would one day be his king consort.

"One day we'll return together, to our home, bathed in rays of gold."

Remembrance of Rennala, Queen of the Full Moon, hewn into the Erdtree. The power of its namesake can be unlocked by the Finger Reader. Alternatively, it can be used to gain a great bounty of runes. In her youth, Rennala was prominent champion who charmed the academy with her lunar magic, becoming its master. She also led the Glintstone Knights and established the house of Caria as royalty.

Remembrance of Starscourge Radahn, hewn into the Erdtree. The power of its namesake can be unlocked by the Finger Reader. Alternatively, it can be used to gain a great bounty of runes. The Red Lion General wielded gravitational powers which he learned in Sellia during his younger days. All so he would never have to abandon his beloved but scrawny steed.

Ancestral spirits exist as a phenomenon beyond the purview of the Erdtree. Life sprouts from death, as it does from birth. Such is the way of the living.

Though born one of the graceless Omen, Morgott took it upon himself to become the Erdtree's protector. He loved not in return, for he was never loved, but nevertheless, love it he did.

A malformed star born in the flightless void far away. Once destroyed an Eternal City and took away their sky. An falling star of ill omen.

"I understand. The road of blasphemy is long and perilous. One cannot walk it unprepared to sin."

Remembrance of Lichdragon Fortissax, hewn into the Erdtree. The power of its namesake can be unlocked by the Finger Reader. Alternatively, it can be used to gain a great bounty of runes. After Godwyn the Golden became the Prince of Death, the ancient dragon fought long and hard against the Death within its companion. Alas, victory was never achieved and its only reward was corruption.

"O trifling giant, mayest thou tend thy flame for eternity."

Remembrance of Mohg, Lord of Blood, hewn into the Erdtree. The power of its namesake can be unlocked by the Finger Reader. Alternatively, it can be used to gain a great bounty of runes. Wishing to raise Miquella to full godhood, Mohg wished to become his consort, taking the role of monarch. But no matter how much of his bloody bedchamber he tried to share, he received no response from the young Empyrean.

Remembrance of Dragonlord Placidusax, hewn into the Erdtree. The power of its namesake can be unlocked by the Finger Reader. Alternatively, it can be used to gain a great bounty of runes. The Dragonlord whose seat lies at the heart of the storm beyond time is said to have been Elden Lord in the age before the Erdtree. Once his god was fled, the lord continued to await its return.

Remembrance of the warrior Hoarah Loux, hewn into the Erdtree. The power of its namesake can be unlocked by the Finger Reader. Alternatively, it can be used to gain a great bounty of runes. When Godfrey, first Elden Lord was robbed of his grace, becoming Tarnished, he took with him his kinfolk and left the Lands Between. After the Long March of the Tarnished came to an end, Godfrey divested himself of kingship, becoming a simple warrior once more.

Remembrance of Malenia, Goddess of Rot, hewn into the Erdtree. The power of its namesake can be unlocked by the Finger Reader. Alternatively, it can be used to gain a great bounty of runes. Miquella and Malenia are both the children of a single god. As such they are both Empyreans, but suffered afflictions from birth. One was cursed with eternal childhood, and the other harbored rot within.
